question: More and more universities in Europe are offering undergraduate courses that are taught exclusively in English. In order to enrol, candidates who are not native English speakers must obtain expensive international language certificates which expire after two years.

Students use these certificates to prove that their English skills are strong enough to study for degrees taught entirely in that language, and it is fair to expect that those who graduate from such courses are as proficient, if not indeed more so, than they were when they first matriculated.

However, many European universities require candidates for master’s degrees in English – including graduates of bachelor’s courses belonging to the same pathway – to provide valid certificates to replace those that have expired. As a result, many students are forced to sit the generic language certification test again, and have to fork out a second time for the privilege.

This requirement constitutes an unjustified barrier to free movement, is at odds with the EU’s goal of fostering fair academic mobility and penalises economically disadvantaged students in particular. In the light of the above: 1.
Does the Commission hold that the aforementioned requirement restricts student mobility, particularly in the EU?
Does it consider this practice to be compatible with the principles of the single market and the mutual recognition of qualifications?
What concrete measures will the Commission implement to grant exemptions to the alumni of courses taught in English in the EU?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (22.12.2025) While the Commission supports initiatives enhancing academic mobility, admission requirements, including language certifications, are determined at national level. This is in line with Article 165 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union1, which places responsibility for the organisation of education systems with Member States.

As such, universities in Member States have the autonomy to set their own admission criteria, including language proficiency standards, as long as they comply with EU law. In accordance with the above, and in line with the principle of institutional autonomy, universities in Member States may therefore require students to demonstrate their proficiency to enrol in English taught courses2.

In addition, the recognition of academic qualifications primarily rests with national authorities. The Commission remains committed to strengthening recognition within the EU, while respecting the Member States’ competences, through non-binding instruments.

Regarding exemptions for alumni of English-taught courses, while the Commission continues to work towards facilitating student mobility and improving accessibility, it primarily operates by encouraging best practices across the EU or offering other relevant support.

For example, students selected to go abroad with the Erasmus+ might undergo a free online language support test, which determines their proficiency in various languages, including English. Additionally, after such assessment students have access to a personalised language learning pathway.
